body_html:
Four governments publish travel advice on medical care in Vietnam: the UK, Australia, Canada and the United States. The pages return to three themes: care in Hanoi is described as better than care elsewhere in the country but can fall short of home standards; the advice is that insurance should cover evacuation; and hospitals may want payment first. This article sets out each theme with its source and date. The advice is written for travellers of those four nationalities.

Hanoi compared with elsewhere

The Government of Canada (updated 19 October 2026) says healthcare standards and availability are generally better in major cities, including Hanoi, while medical care remains limited in smaller cities and remote areas. Smartraveller (updated 24 September 2026) says standards vary and are generally below Australian standards. It adds that foreign private clinics in Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City and Da Nang may not meet Australian standards, and rates care at "most public hospitals" as poor, especially outside Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City.

The United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), on a page last updated 25 August 2026, says that after a serious injury, emergency care may not be available or may not meet United States standards, and that trauma centres are uncommon outside urban areas. The United States Embassy page (no date shown) says care in Vietnam generally falls below United States standards and that even routine injuries may sometimes need evacuation to a regional medical centre. Smartraveller and the United States pages measure against Australian and United States standards, so the ratings cannot be merged into one score.

Insurance first

The UK government (page shows no date) says to check before travelling that the destination can provide the healthcare you may need and that insurance covers local treatment and unexpected medical evacuation, and that the policy covers existing health conditions, an air ambulance, full medical cover and repatriation of remains or of family members. It adds that the British Embassy does not pay medical bills. Smartraveller says insurance "must cover all medical costs overseas, including evacuation", that the Australian Government will not pay those costs, and that exclusions matter: "you might need to pay extra for activities like motorcycling". The CDC advises reviewing what a health plan covers abroad and considering travel health and medical evacuation insurance. Canada advises insurance that covers medical evacuation and hospital stays.

For riders, the UK safety page says to make sure travel insurance covers the planned activity, and Smartraveller says an insurer will likely deny claims from a rider who is unlicensed or lacks the correct licence class. Questions to put to an insurer are in Travel Insurance and Rental Motorbikes in Vietnam: Questions for Your Insurer.

Paying up front and evacuation

Smartraveller says doctors and hospitals expect payment before they treat you, including in an emergency. Some hospitals may talk with the traveller's insurer to secure payment; others may need up-front payment before they start. Without insurance, it says, a traveller "might have to pay thousands of dollars up front for medical care". Canada says public and private facilities may require payment before treatment, and the UK advises contacting your insurer quickly if you are referred to a medical facility for treatment.

On evacuation, Smartraveller says a seriously ill or injured traveller may need to be evacuated to Bangkok or Singapore, and may need evacuation to a major centre even for minor operations. Canada says medical evacuation is very expensive; Smartraveller says it can be.

Calling for help

The UK government says to dial 115 and ask for an ambulance, and the United States Embassy page lists police 113, fire 114 and ambulance 115. Smartraveller says the emergency numbers are operated in Vietnamese only and may be unreliable, with a possible long wait before services arrive. Canada says, in general advice not specific to crash injuries, that ambulance response may be slow in traffic and that a taxi or private vehicle to hospital is an option rather than waiting for an ambulance.

Finding a facility

The United States Embassy page groups its Hanoi list into international clinics and hospitals, private hospitals, public hospitals and specialised hospitals. Its disclaimer says the embassy assumes no responsibility for the professional ability or reputation of the facilities, that the list is neither exclusive nor exhaustive, and that "many of the international medical facilities have foreign English-speaking doctors on staff". Canada says private clinics and hospitals are usually better equipped, can be expensive and usually have qualified staff who speak English or French well.

The UK government's list of medical facilities was updated on 24 June 2022, so it is over four years old. It has 13 Hanoi entries, eight labelled public and five private, as the list classes them. In its English-speaking-staff column five read "yes", four "some" and four "few". The UK says it endorses none of the providers and that the list is not exhaustive and can change at any time. Names and phone numbers are left out here because listings change and both governments disclaim responsibility for, or endorsement of, the facilities. The CDC suggests carrying a list of local doctors and hospitals.

Riding and the medical risk

The UK government says motorbike travel in Vietnam is much riskier than in the UK, advises against hiring a motorbike unless you are an experienced rider, and says to check the bike thoroughly, rent from a reputable organisation and use a good helmet, adding that it is illegal for drivers and passengers to ride without one. The CDC advises avoiding motorbikes, noting that "many crashes are caused by inexperienced motorbike drivers", and always wearing a helmet. Canada advises avoiding driving a motorcycle and having proper insurance and a valid licence. Smartraveller says to ride only if properly licensed and comfortable with local conditions.

The advice therefore runs from a warning to inexperienced riders (UK) to avoiding motorbikes (CDC, Canada). For checks before booking, see Hanoi Motorbike Rental Guide: What to Check Before Booking.

What the advice leaves out

No page gives prices for consultations, treatment, ambulance rides, hospital stays, premiums or evacuation flights. They call care and evacuation expensive, and Smartraveller's "thousands of dollars" is the only cost figure they give for care. No page gives ambulance response times, says which Hanoi hospital suits road injuries, or says what a rental customer's insurance would pay after a crash. The advice does not describe Vietnamese public health insurance or what other nationalities' insurers require. Vaccines, dengue and air quality appear on the pages but are outside this article; see Hanoi Air Quality and Motorbike Plans: Read Official Advisories.

  • GOV.UK (FCDO), Vietnam "Safety and security" page, no date shown. UK safety advice
  • Smartraveller (Australian Government), updated 24 September 2026. Smartraveller Vietnam advice
  • Government of Canada, updated 19 October 2026. Canada Vietnam advice
  • United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Travelers' Health, page last updated 25 August 2026. CDC Vietnam page
  • United States Embassy and Consulate in Vietnam, Medical Assistance page, no date shown. United States Embassy medical assistance
  • GOV.UK (FCDO), list of medical facilities in Hanoi and northern provinces, updated 24 June 2022. UK medical facilities list
